verifiedClaims.claim: the Cornell Law Institute provides a comprehensive overview of limitation periods across legal contexts.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The link (https://www.law.cornell.edu/wex/statute_of_limitations) resolves (HTTP 200, 'statute of limitations | Wex'). The publisher is Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute (LII); there is no 'Cornell Law Institute'.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School — Wex: statute of limitations
verifiedClaims.note: Link is live; only the attribution is wrong. Change the lead-in to 'Cornell Law School's Legal Information Institute provides a concise overview'. Same correction facts-1676 made on the malpractice post.

verifiedClaims.claim: Every personal injury claim in the United States is subject to a statute of limitations — a legal deadline that determines how long you have to file a lawsuit after suffering an injury.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Legal Information Institute, Cornell Law School — Wex: statute of limitations
verifiedClaims.note: Generality; Wex: 'A statute of limitations is any law that bars claims after a certain period of time passes after an injury.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Once the statutory period expires, the court will almost certainly dismiss the case if the defendant raises the defense, no matter how clear the liability or how severe the injuries.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-78-110 ('forever barred'); O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82 ('shall be barred')
verifiedClaims.note: Correctly framed as an affirmative defense the defendant must raise. No figure asserted.

verifiedClaims.claim: It does not prevent you from filing an insurance claim or attempting to negotiate a settlement after the deadline, though practically speaking, your leverage in those negotiations disappears once the insurer knows you can no longer threaten litigation.
verifiedClaims.note: Practice generality; the limitation statutes bar 'actions', not claims to an insurer. No figure asserted.

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, the general statute of limitations for personal injury claims is two years from the date of the injury, as set forth in O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim: 'actions for injuries to the person shall be brought within two years after the right of action accrues'. Matches the writer-profile table. The same section gives one year for injuries to reputation and four years for loss of consortium — optional to add.

verifiedClaims.claim: This two-year window applies to most accident-related claims, including: Car accidents and other motor vehicle collisions, Truck accidents, Motorcycle accidents, Slip and fall injuries, Dog bite claims, Pedestrian accident injuries
verifiedClaims.note: All are 'injuries to the person'; Georgia has no separate dog-bite limitation period.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia also imposes a four-year statute of limitations for property damage claims under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-31.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim: 'Actions for injuries to personalty shall be brought within four years after the right of action accrues.' § 9-3-31 is personal property (a vehicle); damage to real property is § 9-3-30, also four years. The car-accident framing in the next sentence fits § 9-3-31.

verifiedClaims.claim: For wrongful death claims in Georgia, the statute of limitations is also two years under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, running from the date of the decedent's death rather than the date of the initial injury.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33 (2025) and Justia annotations ('Wrongful death action')
verifiedClaims.note: Georgia has no separate wrongful-death limitation statute; courts apply the two-year period of § 9-3-33 running from the death. Consistent with facts-1649. If the tortfeasor has died, § 9-3-93 pauses the period (up to five years) while the estate is unrepresented — optional.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia follows a modified comparative fault rule under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33, which bars recovery if the injured party is 50% or more at fault.
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the writer-profile table ('recover if less than 50% at fault').

verifiedClaims.claim: The general statute of limitations for personal injury claims is three years from the date of injury, as established by S.C. Code § 15-3-530.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim: 'Within three years: ... (5) an action for assault, battery, or any injury to the person or rights of another, not arising on contract'. Under § 15-3-535 the three years run from when the person 'knew or by the exercise of reasonable diligence should have known' of the cause of action — the post's 'from the date of injury' is the usual case, not the rule.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's wrongful death statute of limitations is also three years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530, running from the date of death.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim: '(6) an action under Sections 15-51-10 to 15-51-60 for death by wrongful act, the period to begin to run upon the death of the person'. Pin the cite to § 15-3-530(6).

verifiedClaims.claim: For medical malpractice claims, South Carolina imposes a three-year statute of limitations with a maximum six-year statute of repose under S.C. Code § 15-3-545, meaning no claim can be filed more than six years after the treatment, regardless of when the injury was discovered.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 15-3-545(A): three years from the treatment or from discovery, 'not to exceed six years from date of occurrence'. But (B) foreign-object and misplaced-appliance cases run two years from discovery with no six-year cap (only a three-year floor), and (D) tolls the period for minors up to seven years. 'Regardless of when the injury was discovered' overstates it.
verifiedClaims.note: Minimal edit: 'meaning that, apart from foreign-object cases, no claim can be filed more than six years after the treatment, however late the injury was discovered'. Consistent with facts-1824.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina also follows a modified comparative fault system, barring recovery if the plaintiff is 51% or more at fault.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991) (verified facts-1756)
verifiedClaims.note: Matches the writer-profile table. If an authority is added it must be Nelson, never § 15-38-15.

verifiedClaims.claim: Medical malpractice | 2 years (5-year repose) | 3 years (6-year repose)
verifiedClaims.note: Comparison-table row. Both figures verified. Georgia's two years run from the injury or death with no discovery rule; the five-year repose runs from the negligent act.

verifiedClaims.claim: Property damage | 4 years (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-31) | 3 years
verifiedClaims.note: South Carolina: three years for 'damage to real property' (3) and 'injuring any goods or chattels' (4). Optional: add '(S.C. Code § 15-3-530)' to the cell.

verifiedClaims.claim: Government claims notice | Ante-litem notice required | 2 years to file (S.C. Code § 15-78-110); 3 if a verified claim is filed within 1 year
verifiedClaims.note: Both cells verified. Optional precision in the Georgia cell: 'Ante litem notice — 6 months (city), 12 months (county or state)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: If the injured person is a minor at the time of the accident, the statute of limitations is generally tolled until they reach the age of 18. In Georgia, minors then have two years from their 18th birthday to file. In South Carolina, the three-year clock begins at age 18.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: correct for ordinary claims — § 9-3-90(b) gives a minor 'the same time after he or she reaches the age of 18 years' as other persons, so the 20th birthday (medical malpractice is different: § 9-3-73). South Carolina: wrong — § 15-3-40 excludes the time of minority but the period 'cannot be extended ... in any case longer than one year after the disability ceases', so the deadline is the 19th birthday, or three years from the injury if that is later (malpractice: tolled at most seven years, § 15-3-545(D)).
verifiedClaims.note: Core error, same one facts-1704 corrected on the minors post. A South Carolina reader who waits until 20 is time-barred. Replace the last sentence with: 'In South Carolina the extension is capped at one year after the child turns 18, so the deadline is the 19th birthday — or three years from the injury, if that is later (S.C. Code § 15-3-40).' Add '(O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90)' to the Georgia sentence.

verifiedClaims.claim: If the injured person is mentally incapacitated at the time of the injury, the statute may be tolled for the duration of the incapacity. This can apply to victims who suffer traumatic brain injuries that prevent them from understanding their legal rights.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: § 9-3-90(a) — persons 'legally incompetent because of intellectual disability or mental illness' when the action accrues get the same time after the disability is removed; § 9-3-91 also stops the clock for a disability that arises after accrual if not voluntarily caused. Georgia courts toll for mental, not physical, disability (Chapman v. Burks, 183 Ga. App. 103 (1987), annotation to § 9-3-91); medical-malpractice claims are excluded (§ 9-3-73). South Carolina: § 15-3-40(2) 'insane' — but the extension is capped at five years and at one year after the disability ceases.
verifiedClaims.note: Direction is right; add the South Carolina cap: 'In Georgia the clock waits until the incapacity is removed (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90); South Carolina caps the extension at five years, and at one year after the incapacity ends (S.C. Code § 15-3-40).' The TBI example is fine — the test is legal incompetence, not the injury type.

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-94, if the defendant leaves the state after causing the injury, the time spent outside Georgia does not count toward the statute of limitations. South Carolina has a similar tolling provision for absent defendants.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 9-3-94 (2025) still reads: 'Unless otherwise provided by law, if a defendant removes from this state, the time of his absence from the state until he returns to reside shall not be counted or estimated in his favor.' But the annotations limit it sharply: it applies 'only if removal makes it impossible to perfect service on defendant' (Railey v. State Farm, 129 Ga. App. 875 (1973)); the two-year personal-injury period 'was not tolled ... since there was no showing that the defendants could not have been served with process pursuant to the long-arm statute' (Towns v. Brown, 177 Ga. App. 504 (1986)); a driver who moved to Maryland did not toll it (Dickson v. Amick, 291 Ga. App. 557 (2008)); temporary absence never counts. South Carolina: § 15-3-30 excludes the absence only where the defendant departs 'and reside[s] out of this State or remain[s] continuously absent therefrom for the space of one year or more'.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 9-3-94 (2025) and Justia annotations; S.C. Code § 15-3-30
verifiedClaims.note: As written it promises a tolling that Georgia courts almost never grant in a car-accident case, because an out-of-state driver can be served under the long-arm and nonresident-motorist statutes. Rewrite: 'Georgia's tolling statute for defendants who move away (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-94) rarely helps in an accident case: courts apply it only when the move actually makes the defendant impossible to serve, and an out-of-state driver can still be served under Georgia's long-arm statute. South Carolina's version (S.C. Code § 15-3-30) excludes only absences of a year or more. Do not count on either.'

verifiedClaims.claim: If the defendant actively conceals the cause of injury or commits fraud to prevent the plaintiff from discovering the claim, courts may toll the deadline in both states.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia: statutory — O.C.G.A. § 9-3-96 tolls the period until the plaintiff discovers the fraud (it does not toll the § 9-3-71(b) medical-malpractice repose, facts-1676). South Carolina: concealment is handled by the discovery rule itself — § 15-3-535 runs the three years from when the plaintiff 'knew or by the exercise of reasonable diligence should have known' of the claim; § 15-3-530(7) covers fraud actions.
verifiedClaims.note: Substance right; add the citations: 'In Georgia this is statutory (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-96); in South Carolina the discovery rule (S.C. Code § 15-3-535) does the same work.'

verifiedClaims.claim: However, both Georgia and South Carolina recognize the discovery rule in certain situations — particularly medical malpractice and toxic exposure cases — where the injury may not be immediately apparent.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina: yes, and broader than 'certain situations' — § 15-3-535 applies the knew-or-should-have-known rule to every § 15-3-530(5) personal-injury action, and § 15-3-545(A) applies it to medical malpractice. Georgia: no general discovery rule, and none for medical malpractice — § 9-3-71(a) runs from the injury or death, and 'the controlling factor is the date of the negligent act' (facts-1676, Justia annotations). Georgia's only discovery-based accrual rules are the foreign-object statute (§ 9-3-72: one year after the act 'is discovered'), fraud tolling (§ 9-3-96) and the judge-made continuing-tort doctrine for ongoing exposure (annotations to § 9-3-33).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-3-535; O.C.G.A. §§ 9-3-71, 9-3-72, 9-3-96; Justia annotations to § 9-3-33 ('continuing tort')
verifiedClaims.note: Most consequential error on the page: it tells Georgia readers a discovery rule exists for malpractice. Rewrite the section opening: 'South Carolina has a true discovery rule: for any personal injury claim the three years run from when you knew or reasonably should have known you had a claim (S.C. Code § 15-3-535), and the same applies to medical malpractice (§ 15-3-545). Georgia does not. Its two-year clock runs from the injury, and for medical malpractice from the date of the negligent act, whether or not you knew about it (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71). Georgia's narrow exceptions are a foreign object left in the body (one year from discovery, § 9-3-72), fraud by the defendant (§ 9-3-96), and ongoing exposure treated as a continuing tort.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Under the discovery rule, the statute of limitations begins when the injured person knew or reasonably should have known about the injury and its potential cause.
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate statement of South Carolina's rule ('knew or by the exercise of reasonable diligence should have known that he had a cause of action'). Attribute it to South Carolina once the preceding sentence is fixed.

verifiedClaims.claim: For example, if a surgeon leaves a foreign object inside a patient, the clock may not start until the patient discovers or reasonably should have discovered the object, even if the surgery occurred years earlier.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: True in both states, but by specific statutes, not the general discovery rule: Georgia § 9-3-72 — one year after the negligent act 'is discovered' (chemical compounds, fixation devices and prosthetics excluded); South Carolina § 15-3-545(B) — two years 'from date of discovery or when it reasonably ought to have been discovered', never less than three years after the placement.
verifiedClaims.note: Add the periods: 'one year from discovery in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-72), two years from discovery in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-545(B))'.

verifiedClaims.claim: However, both states impose statutes of repose that set an absolute outer limit. In Georgia, the medical malpractice statute of repose is five years under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71. In South Carolina, it is six years under S.C. Code § 15-3-545. These hard deadlines cannot be extended by the discovery rule.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The five- and six-year figures are right (§ 9-3-71(b); § 15-3-545(A)). But the paragraph pairs them with the foreign-object example, and foreign-object cases are the one place neither repose applies: Georgia § 9-3-72 says 'The limitations of Code Section 9-3-71 shall not apply where a foreign object has been left in a patient's body', and South Carolina's six-year cap sits in § 15-3-545(A), which excludes '(B)' foreign-object actions. Georgia's repose is also unaffected by § 9-3-96 fraud tolling (facts-1676).
verifiedClaims.note: Rewrite the last sentence: 'These hard deadlines cannot be extended by late discovery or, in Georgia, by fraud — the foreign-object statutes above are the one exception.'

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, injured workers must report the injury to their employer within 30 days and file a claim with the State Board of Workers' Compensation within one year of the injury under O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82.
verifiedClaims.note: Both verified verbatim: § 34-9-80 'within 30 days after the accident'; § 34-9-82(a) 'barred unless a claim therefor is filed within one year after injury' (or one year after the last employer-furnished treatment / two years after the last weekly benefit). The 30-day notice belongs to § 34-9-80 — add that cite after '30 days'.

verifiedClaims.claim: In South Carolina, the deadline to file is two years from the injury under S.C. Code § 42-15-40.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim: 'barred unless a claim is filed with the commission within two years after an accident'. Optional parallel to the Georgia sentence: notice to the employer within 90 days (§ 42-15-20(B)).

verifiedClaims.claim: Product liability claims in Georgia follow the standard two-year personal injury deadline but are subject to a 10-year statute of repose under O.C.G.A. § 51-1-11 from the date the product was first sold.
verifiedClaims.note: Ten years 'from the date of the first sale for use or consumption'; applies to strict-liability and (with disease/birth-defect and wilful-misconduct exceptions) negligence claims.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina applies the three-year limitation with its own product liability repose provisions.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina has no product-liability statute of repose: Title 15, Chapter 73 (Products Liability) and Chapter 3 (Limitation of Civil Actions) contain none (scstatehouse.gov text read 2026-09-25; facts-1864). The three years run under the discovery rule, § 15-3-535.
verifiedClaims.note: Replace with: 'South Carolina applies the three-year limitation, running from when the injury was or should have been discovered (S.C. Code § 15-3-535), and has no product liability statute of repose.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Maritime injury claims and boating accident cases may fall under federal maritime law, which imposes a three-year statute of limitations regardless of the state. Jones Act claims for injured seamen also carry a three-year deadline.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim: § 30106 'a civil action for damages for personal injury or death arising out of a maritime tort must be brought within 3 years after the cause of action arose'; the Jones Act applies the railway-employee (FELA) rules, and 45 U.S.C. § 56 requires suit 'within three years from the day the cause of action accrued'. Add '(46 U.S.C. § 30106)' after 'regardless of the state'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5, claims against Georgia municipalities require an ante-litem notice within six months of the incident. Claims against the state itself require notice under O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26 within 12 months.
verifiedClaims.note: Both verified in the sibling packs. The post skips counties: § 36-11-1, 12 months. Add one clause: 'and against a county within 12 months (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Failing to provide this notice within the required timeframe bars the claim entirely, even if the general statute of limitations has not expired.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: O.C.G.A. § 50-21-26 (notice is jurisdictional, facts-1724); § 36-11-1 ('or the same are barred')

verifiedClaims.claim: Under the South Carolina Tort Claims Act, claims against government entities must be filed within two years of the incident (S.C. Code § 15-78-110). South Carolina requires no pre-suit notice: filing a verified claim with the agency within one year is optional, and doing so extends the deadline to three years (S.C. Code § 15-78-80).
verifiedClaims.note: Verified verbatim: § 15-78-110 two years 'after the date the loss was or should have been discovered', three if a claim was first filed; § 15-78-80(a) a verified claim 'may be filed', (d) 'If filed, the claim must be received within one year'. Matches the writer-profile table. Minor: the two years run from discovery of the loss, not strictly 'the incident'.

verifiedClaims.claim: There are also caps on the amount of damages recoverable against government defendants in South Carolina.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified: $300,000 per person and $600,000 per occurrence ($1.2 million where the tort is a government-employed physician's or dentist's); no punitive damages or prejudgment interest. Optional to add the figures with the cite.

verifiedClaims.claim: The defendant will file a motion to dismiss based on the expired statute of limitations; The court will almost certainly grant the dismissal; You lose the ability to pursue compensation through the court system; Insurance companies will refuse to negotiate because they know you cannot sue; Your attorney may be unable to take the case on a contingency fee basis
verifiedClaims.note: Procedural generalities, no figures. Nothing in either state revives a barred claim.

verifiedClaims.claim: In rare circumstances, courts may apply equitable tolling if the plaintiff can demonstrate extraordinary circumstances that prevented timely filing. However, these exceptions are narrow and difficult to prove.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Verified for South Carolina: the Supreme Court applied equitable tolling in Hooper v. Ebenezer Senior Services & Rehabilitation Center, 386 S.C. 108 (2009), 'under the unique circumstances of this case', and the Court of Appeals below said the doctrine 'is reserved for extraordinary circumstances' and 'rarely applied'. For Georgia the tolling grounds are the statutory ones in O.C.G.A. §§ 9-3-90 to 9-3-99 (minority, incapacity, absence, estates, fraud); no Georgia equitable-tolling authority was verified.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Hooper v. Ebenezer Senior Servs. & Rehab. Ctr., 386 S.C. 108, 687 S.E.2d 29 (2009)
verifiedClaims.note: Attribute it: 'South Carolina courts have applied equitable tolling in rare, extraordinary circumstances (Hooper v. Ebenezer Senior Services, 2009); Georgia's exceptions are the statutory tolling rules above.'

verifiedClaims.claim: At Roden Law, our attorneys handle personal injury cases on a contingency fee basis — you pay nothing unless we recover compensation for you.
verifiedClaims.note: Firm statement, not a legal claim. The tel: link +1-844-737-8587 spells 1-844-RESULTS correctly.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia allows two years to file personal injury lawsuits under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33, while South Carolina allows three years under S.C. Code § 15-3-530.
Exceptions include tolling for minors, mental incapacity, and the discovery rule.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Minors and mental incapacity toll in both states (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90; S.C. Code § 15-3-40, capped). The discovery rule is South Carolina's (§ 15-3-535); Georgia has none for ordinary injury or malpractice claims.
verifiedClaims.note: Renders above the article. Rewrite: 'Exceptions include tolling for minors and mental incapacity in both states, and South Carolina's discovery rule — Georgia has no general discovery rule.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Government claims run on shorter clocks — ante litem notice within six months for a Georgia city, and a two-year filing deadline under South Carolina's Tort Claims Act. Missing the deadline permanently bars recovery.
How long you have to file a personal injury lawsuit in Georgia and South Carolina, plus the exceptions that shorten or extend the deadline.
verifiedClaims.note: No factual claim; publishes as the Article description.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia has a two-year statute of limitations for most personal injury claims under O.C.G.A. § 9-3-33. The clock generally starts on the date of the injury, though exceptions like the discovery rule may apply in certain cases.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Two years under § 9-3-33 is right. Georgia has no general discovery rule; the exceptions that move the deadline are statutory tolling (minors and incapacity § 9-3-90, fraud § 9-3-96) plus the foreign-object rule (§ 9-3-72) and the continuing-tort doctrine for ongoing exposure.
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Rewrite the second sentence: 'The clock generally starts on the date of the injury; Georgia has no general discovery rule, but the deadline is paused for minors and people who are legally incompetent (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90) and when the defendant's fraud hid the claim (§ 9-3-96).'

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina allows three years from the date of injury to file a personal injury lawsuit under S.C. Code § 15-3-530. This applies to car accidents, slip and falls, and most other accident-related claims.
verifiedClaims.note: Optional precision: 'from the date of injury — or from when you knew or reasonably should have known of it (S.C. Code § 15-3-535)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: If you miss the filing deadline, the court will almost certainly dismiss your case. You lose the right to pursue compensation through litigation, and insurance companies will refuse to negotiate because they know you cannot sue.
verifiedClaims.note: Generality consistent with the 'forever barred' language of § 15-78-110 and 'shall be barred' of § 34-9-82.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Both Georgia and South Carolina recognize tolling exceptions for minors, mentally incapacitated individuals, defendants who leave the state, and cases involving fraud or concealment. The discovery rule may also extend the deadline when injuries are not immediately apparent.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Minors and incapacity: both states (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90; S.C. Code § 15-3-40, capped at one year after the disability ends and five years for incapacity). Absence: both have statutes (§ 9-3-94; § 15-3-30) but Georgia applies it only when the move makes service impossible, and South Carolina only for absences of a year or more. Fraud: Georgia § 9-3-96; South Carolina via § 15-3-535. Discovery rule: South Carolina only (§ 15-3-535); Georgia has none apart from foreign objects (§ 9-3-72) and continuing torts.
verifiedClaims.note: Publishes as FAQPage structured data. Rewrite: 'Yes. Both states pause the clock for minors and people who are legally incompetent, and when the defendant's fraud concealed the claim. South Carolina also has a discovery rule that starts the three years when you knew or should have known of the injury (S.C. Code § 15-3-535); Georgia does not. Tolling for a defendant who leaves the state exists on paper in both states but rarely applies, because an out-of-state driver can still be served.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Wrongful death claims follow the same general deadlines: two years in Georgia and three years in South Carolina. The clock starts on the date of the person's death, not necessarily the date of the initial injury.
verifiedClaims.note: South Carolina's rule is verbatim in § 15-3-530(6): 'the period to begin to run upon the death'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Yes. Georgia requires an ante-litem notice within six months for municipal claims under O.C.G.A. § 36-33-5 and within 12 months for state claims. South Carolina requires no pre-suit notice, but the Tort Claims Act shortens the filing deadline to two years (S.C. Code § 15-78-110); filing a verified claim within one year is optional and extends it to three.
verifiedClaims.note: Fully verified. Optional: 'and 12 months for county claims (O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1)'.

recommendedEdits: Discovery Rule section: rewrite the opening paragraph so the discovery rule is attributed to South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-535 for all personal injury; § 15-3-545 for malpractice) and Georgia is stated to have NO general or malpractice discovery rule (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-71 runs from the injury/act); list Georgia's narrow exceptions as foreign objects (§ 9-3-72, one year from discovery), fraud (§ 9-3-96) and continuing torts.

Discovery Rule section, repose paragraph: change 'These hard deadlines cannot be extended by the discovery rule' to note the foreign-object exception in both states (§ 9-3-72 removes § 9-3-71's limits entirely; § 15-3-545(B) has no six-year cap) and that Georgia's repose is also unaffected by fraud tolling.
Foreign-object example: add the actual periods — one year from discovery in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-72), two years from discovery in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 15-3-545(B)).

Minority (Under 18): replace 'In South Carolina, the three-year clock begins at age 18' with the one-year cap — deadline is the 19th birthday, or three years from the injury if later (S.C. Code § 15-3-40); add '(O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90)' to the Georgia sentence and a parenthetical that malpractice claims run on a shorter clock (§ 9-3-73).
Mental Incapacity: add citations (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-90; S.C. Code § 15-3-40) and the South Carolina cap — no more than five years, and no more than one year after the incapacity ends.

Defendant Leaves the State: rewrite to say § 9-3-94 applies only when the move makes the defendant impossible to serve (an out-of-state driver can still be served under the long-arm statute), and cite South Carolina's § 15-3-30 (absences of a year or more); tell readers not to rely on it.
Fraud or Concealment: add 'O.C.G.A. § 9-3-96' for Georgia and note South Carolina reaches the same result through the discovery rule (§ 15-3-535).
South Carolina medical malpractice sentence: qualify 'regardless of when the injury was discovered' with 'apart from foreign-object cases'.

Maritime paragraph: add '(46 U.S.C. § 30106)' after 'regardless of the state' and '(46 U.S.C. § 30104; 45 U.S.C. § 56)' after the Jones Act sentence.
Georgia Ante-Litem Notice: add counties — 12 months under O.C.G.A. § 36-11-1.
